items.prompt: Northwind has a beautifully designed Figma file showing exactly what the primary button should look like, but engineers still hardcode slightly different blues across screens. Is that Figma file a design system?
choices: Yes — a design system is fundamentally a design artifact, so a well-made Figma file qualifies
No — a design system is what engineers actually import and reuse in code; a reference file that isn't wired into the codebase is documentation of intent, not a source of truth
Yes, as long as the Figma file is kept up to date by the design team
No, because Figma is the wrong tool — only code-first tools count
items.explanation: A design system has to be the thing that's actually consumed — tokens and components engineers import — not just a reference an engineer could look at and then reimplement slightly differently. A Figma file with no code counterpart is a plan for a design system, not the thing itself.
items.reference:
Style guide PDF/Figma

Reference only — engineers can drift from it

Design system

Imported code — drifting from it means the build breaks

Why: if it isn't the thing that's actually imported and reused, it isn't a design system yet.

items.prompt: Which of these is the best one-sentence description of what a design system actually is?
choices: A shared, named, versioned set of visual decisions and the reusable components built on them, so no one reinvents them per screen
A committee that approves every new screen before it ships
A single company-wide brand color palette, nothing more
A style guide document that designers reference but engineers don't need to touch
items.explanation: The core of a design system is that visual decisions are made once, named, and reused — via tokens and components engineers actually build with — rather than remade (and inevitably drifted) on every screen.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'our design system is just whatever's in the Sketch file, everyone should just look at it before building a screen.' What's the risk in that setup specifically?
choices: There's no risk — Sketch files are a perfectly reliable single source of truth
Nothing stops an engineer from looking at the file, misremembering a detail, or skipping the check under deadline pressure — there's no mechanism forcing consistency, only a hope for it
The risk is only that Sketch is a paid tool
The risk only applies to junior engineers, not experienced ones
items.explanation: 'Look at the file and match it' relies on memory and diligence under pressure, with no structural enforcement — exactly the gap that let Northwind's four teams each rebuild a slightly different Button. A design system closes that gap by making reuse the path of least resistance, not an optional extra step.

items.prompt: `color.primary` is defined once and referenced by both the `Button` and `Card` components. Which layer does `color.primary` belong to, and which layer do `Button` and `Card` belong to?
choices: `color.primary` is a component; `Button`/`Card` are tokens
`color.primary` is a design token (a named value); `Button` and `Card` are components (reusable UI built from tokens)
They're the same layer — tokens and components are just two names for the same thing
`color.primary` is a component library; `Button`/`Card` are design tokens
items.explanation: Tokens are named values (a color, a spacing unit); components are the reusable, assembled UI pieces built on top of those values. `color.primary` has no visual shape of its own — `Button` and `Card` are what actually render, using that value.
items.reference:
Token

A named value: color.primary = #2563EB

Component

Reusable UI built from tokens: Button, Card

Why: tokens are values; components are the assembled pieces that consume those values.

items.prompt: An engineer says 'we don't need a component library, tokens are enough — as long as everyone uses `var(--color-primary)` instead of hardcoding hex values, we're consistent.' What's missing from that plan?
choices: Nothing — tokens alone fully solve the drift problem

Tokens fix the *value* problem but not the *assembly* problem — nothing stops one screen from getting the border-radius or disabled-state token right and another from forgetting it entirely, which is exactly what caused Northwind's checkout bug
Tokens are actually unnecessary if you have components
Nothing is missing, but only for color tokens specifically
items.explanation: Tokens centralize values, but a screen still has to remember to use all of them correctly and together. A component library forces every consumer to get the whole set — color, radius, spacing, disabled state — right by construction, because they're importing one implementation instead of reassembling the pieces by hand each time.
items.reference:
Token

A named value: color.primary = #2563EB

Component

Reusable UI built from tokens: Button, Card

Why: tokens are values; components are the assembled pieces that consume those values.

items.prompt: What makes something a 'design token' rather than just a value written in a stylesheet?
choices: It has to be a color specifically — spacing and radius values don't count as tokens
It's a named, reusable value defined exactly once, referenced everywhere it's used — not copy-pasted or retyped per screen
It has to live in a JSON file — CSS custom properties don't count
Any value used more than twice automatically becomes a token
items.explanation: The defining property of a token is the name-and-reference structure: define `color.primary` once, and every consumer points at the name, not a re-typed copy of the value. Tokens cover any repeated design decision — color, spacing, radius, type scale — not just color, and they can be authored in JSON and compiled to CSS custom properties, platform code, or both.
items.reference:
Token = name + value, defined once. color.primary → #2563EB, referenced everywhere, never retyped.

Why: the name is what makes it a single source of truth — the value itself could be anything.

items.prompt: `radius.md = 8px` is used by both the Button and the Card component's corners. What kind of design decision does this token represent?
choices: A color decision
A spacing/sizing decision — tokens cover any repeated visual value, not just colors
It's not a real token because it isn't a color
A component, not a token
items.explanation: Tokens generalize to any named, reusable value: colors, spacing, corner radii, type sizes, shadows. `radius.md` follows the exact same name-once-reference-everywhere pattern as a color token — the category doesn't change what makes it a token.
items.reference:
Token = name + value, defined once. color.primary → #2563EB, referenced everywhere, never retyped.

Why: the name is what makes it a single source of truth — the value itself could be anything.

items.prompt: Two engineers each write `background-color: #2563EB;` directly in their own screen's CSS, without referencing any shared name. Are they using a design token?
choices: Yes, because they happen to use the same value

No — a token requires a shared name that both reference; two people independently typing the same hex is a coincidence, not a source of truth, and it will drift the moment one of them needs to change it
Yes, as long as they're on the same team
It depends only on whether the value is documented somewhere
items.explanation: Matching values by coincidence isn't a token — it's exactly the setup that caused Northwind's drift. A token requires the reference to be shared, so a single edit to the name's definition updates every consumer; two independent hardcodes will inevitably diverge the first time only one of them gets updated.
items.reference:
Token = name + value, defined once. color.primary → #2563EB, referenced everywhere, never retyped.

Why: the name is what makes it a single source of truth — the value itself could be anything.

items.prompt: Which of these is the clearest sign that something calling itself a 'design system' is actually just documentation of one?

The code that ships to production doesn't import anything from it — engineers read it and then retype the decisions by hand
It was created by the design team rather than engineering
It includes color palettes but not typography
items.explanation: The test isn't how polished or well-branded the reference material is — it's whether production code actually consumes it. If engineers read a guide and then hand-type the values, every retyping is a fresh opportunity for drift, which is exactly the failure mode a real design system exists to close.

items.prompt: Northwind's design team keeps a beautiful internal wiki page listing 'our official colors,' but no code references it directly. Six months later, the wiki page is two rebrands out of date. What does this show?
choices: That the wiki page should have been updated more often, but the underlying approach was sound
That documentation with no code dependency has no mechanism forcing it to stay accurate — nothing breaks when it drifts out of sync, so it silently does
That wikis are always a bad tool for design decisions
That this specific team was unusually careless compared to others
items.explanation: A reference nothing depends on has no feedback loop keeping it honest — it can drift silently for months because nothing fails when it does. A token that's actually imported can't drift the same way: change the definition, and every consumer updates or the build points at something visibly wrong.

items.prompt: Northwind's app had zero visible drift when it was 3 screens built by one designer and one engineer. Two years and 40 screens later, the audit found six shades of blue. What best explains the change?
choices: The original designer simply became worse at their job over time
More screens and more people touching them, with no shared source of truth, reliably produces more drift — one person can hold consistency in their head, dozens of people across squads can't
Blue is an unusually hard color to keep consistent compared to other colors
The company's design tools got worse over the two years
items.explanation: At small scale, one person's memory functions as an informal single source of truth. As team size and screen count grow, the number of people making independent micro-decisions grows too, and nothing was forcing them to reference a shared definition — so small, individually reasonable choices compound into visible inconsistency.
items.reference:
1 designer, 3 screens: consistency held informally, in one person's memory.

5 designers, 40 screens: no single memory can hold it — drift becomes inevitable without a shared, referenced source of truth.

Why: scale doesn't cause drift by itself — the absence of a shared reference at scale does.

items.prompt: A founder asks: 'why didn't we need a design system when we were a 3-screen startup?' What's the accurate answer?
choices: Small apps never need consistency, only large ones do
At that scale, one person's memory effectively served as the single source of truth — the need for an explicit, shared one grows with team size and screen count, not with app 'importance'
Design systems were simply not invented yet at that stage of the company
It was luck, with no underlying reason
items.explanation: A design system's value is proportional to how many independent people and screens are making visual decisions without seeing each other's work. One person building three screens doesn't need an explicit shared source of truth because there's no coordination problem yet — the problem appears exactly when that stops being true.
items.reference:
1 designer, 3 screens: consistency held informally, in one person's memory.

5 designers, 40 screens: no single memory can hold it — drift becomes inevitable without a shared, referenced source of truth.

Why: scale doesn't cause drift by itself — the absence of a shared reference at scale does.

items.prompt: Which factor combination is most predictive of visual drift, based on Northwind's story?
choices: High screen count alone, regardless of team size
High team/squad count with low cross-team communication, combined with no shared, referenced source of truth — screen count on its own isn't the driver
Using CSS instead of a design tool
Having more than one product manager
items.explanation: It's specifically the combination of many independent decision-makers (squads that don't talk daily) and no shared reference that produces drift — a single team, however large its screen count, that all shares one component library doesn't have this problem the same way.
items.reference:
1 designer, 3 screens: consistency held informally, in one person's memory.

5 designers, 40 screens: no single memory can hold it — drift becomes inevitable without a shared, referenced source of truth.

Why: scale doesn't cause drift by itself — the absence of a shared reference at scale does.

items.prompt: In the chain `blue.500 = #2563EB` → `color.primary = blue.500` → `button.background = color.primary`, which token is the global token?
choices: `button.background`, because it's the one that actually renders
`blue.500` — the raw palette value with no role or component attached yet
`color.primary`, because it's in the middle
All three are global tokens, they're just named differently
items.explanation: Global tokens hold raw values with no opinion about where they're used — `blue.500` is just a hex code. `color.primary` is an alias that attaches a role to that value, and `button.background` is a component token that points a specific UI slot at that role.
items.reference:
Global: blue.500 = #2563EB (raw value)
Alias: color.primary = blue.500 (a role)
Component: button.background = color.primary (one slot)

items.prompt: What's the purpose of `button.background = color.primary` as a separate layer, instead of just having `Button` reference `color.primary` directly in its code?
choices: There's no real purpose — it's an unnecessary extra step

It gives Button's specific visual slot its own name, so if a future design decision says 'buttons should be a different shade than other primary-colored elements,' only `button.background` needs to be repointed — `color.primary` and everything else referencing it stays untouched
It makes the CSS file smaller
It's only useful for accessibility, not for design consistency
items.explanation: The component-token layer exists so a single component's visual decision can later diverge from the general-purpose alias without a hardcoded reference to that alias scattered through the component's code — it's one more layer of indirection that keeps 'what should change when X changes' scoped to exactly the right blast radius.
items.reference:
Global: blue.500 = #2563EB (raw value)
Alias: color.primary = blue.500 (a role)
Component: button.background = color.primary (one slot)

items.prompt: Which statement correctly orders the three token layers from most general to most specific?
choices: Component tokens → alias tokens → global tokens
Global tokens (raw values) → alias tokens (roles pointing at globals) → component tokens (one component's slot pointing at an alias)
Alias tokens → global tokens → component tokens
There's no meaningful order — all three layers are interchangeable
items.explanation: The layering runs from raw and general (global) to role-based (alias) to specific-and-scoped (component) — each layer references the one before it, never the other way around, which is what lets a change at the global layer fan out predictably.
items.reference:
Global: blue.500 = #2563EB (raw value)
Alias: color.primary = blue.500 (a role)
Component: button.background = color.primary (one slot)

items.prompt: Marketing rebrands the primary blue to a warmer shade. In a properly layered system, which single line has to change?
choices: Every component's CSS file needs a manual edit
Only the global token's raw value — `blue.500`'s hex — because every alias and component token downstream is a reference to it, not a copy
Only the alias token, `color.primary`, needs a new name
Nothing changes automatically — every screen still needs to be found and updated
items.explanation: Because `color.primary` points at `blue.500` by reference, and `button.background` points at `color.primary` by reference, updating the one raw value at the global layer resolves correctly everywhere downstream — that's the entire payoff of not hardcoding values at any layer above the global one.
items.reference:
Change blue.500 once → color.primary and button.background both resolve to the new value automatically, with zero edits to either.

Why: references, not copies, are what make a one-line rebrand possible.

items.prompt: A system where `button.background` is hardcoded to `#2563EB` directly, instead of referencing `color.primary`, breaks which part of the rebrand story?
choices: Nothing breaks — hardcoding the resolved value is equivalent to referencing it

The one-line-edit property breaks: a rebrand now requires finding and changing every place that hardcoded the value, exactly like Northwind's original problem, just with tokens instead of raw component code
It only breaks dark mode, not rebrands
It breaks only if the component is used on more than one screen
items.explanation: Hardcoding a resolved value anywhere in the chain — even inside a 'token' — reintroduces the exact find-and-replace problem the layering exists to prevent. The layers only pay off if every level above global genuinely references the level below it, rather than copying its current value.
items.reference:
Change blue.500 once → color.primary and button.background both resolve to the new value automatically, with zero edits to either.

Why: references, not copies, are what make a one-line rebrand possible.

items.prompt: Why does `color.primary` exist as a separate alias token instead of every component just referencing `blue.500` directly?
choices: It doesn't matter — `color.primary` and `blue.500` are functionally identical and interchangeable

`color.primary` names a *role* ('whatever we've decided primary means') rather than a specific value — if the company later decides primary should be a different global color entirely, only the alias's target changes, not the meaning components rely on
Alias tokens are purely a naming convention with no functional benefit
`blue.500` is deprecated and should never be used anywhere
items.explanation: The alias layer separates 'what role does this play' from 'what raw value currently fills that role.' A component asking for `color.primary` is asking a question about meaning, not about a specific hex — which is exactly what lets that meaning's answer change without touching the component.
items.reference:
Global token

A raw value: blue.500

Alias token

A role pointing at a value: color.primary

items.prompt: A dark mode toggle needs `color.text.default` to resolve to a light gray on dark backgrounds instead of the near-black used on light backgrounds. Which layer makes this a clean swap rather than a component-by-component rewrite?
choices: The component layer, by hardcoding two versions of every component
The alias layer — `color.text.default` can point at a different global value per theme, and every component referencing that alias name resolves correctly without any component code changing
It requires editing global tokens directly inside each component file
Dark mode has nothing to do with the token layers
items.explanation: Just like a rebrand, a theme swap works by changing what an alias resolves to, not by touching every consumer. `color.text.default` stays the same name in both themes; only the global value it points at differs — the same mechanism that made the rebrand a one-line change makes dark mode a theme-level swap.
items.reference:
Global token

A raw value: blue.500

Alias token

A role pointing at a value: color.primary

items.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a global token to what an alias token adds on top of it?
choices: Global: 'blue.500 = #2563EB' (a raw value); Alias: 'color.primary = blue.500' (attaches the meaning 'primary' to that value)
Global and alias tokens are the same thing, just at different files
Global: 'color.primary'; Alias: 'blue.500' — the order is reversed
Alias tokens replace global tokens entirely and make them unnecessary
items.explanation: A global token is a value with no attached meaning; an alias token attaches a role or meaning ('primary', 'danger', 'text-default') to one of those values by reference. The alias is what components should actually ask for, because it survives the underlying value changing.
items.reference:
Global token

A raw value: blue.500

Alias token

A role pointing at a value: color.primary

items.prompt: Who typically owns changes to a component token like `button.background-disabled`, versus a global token like `blue.500`?
choices: Both are owned by the same person, on the same review cadence, with no distinction
The component owner revises component tokens whenever that component changes, while global tokens change rarely and require broader design-system-team sign-off, since they fan out much further
Component tokens can never be changed once set
Global tokens are owned by individual engineers, component tokens by the CEO
items.explanation: Component tokens are scoped to one component's specific slots, so revising them is a narrow, frequent, low-risk change. Global tokens fan out to everything downstream, so they change rarely and deliberately — the ownership split mirrors the blast radius of each layer.
items.reference:
Component tokens: narrow blast radius, one component, changes often.

Global tokens: wide blast radius, everything downstream, changes rarely and deliberately.

items.prompt: Why does `button.background-disabled` get its own component token instead of every disabled state across the app just reusing `color.text.default` at reduced opacity ad hoc?
choices: It doesn't matter — any approach to disabled states is equally maintainable

Naming the disabled state as its own token makes it an explicit, checkable part of the component's definition — the exact detail that silently went missing in Northwind's checkout bug is much harder to omit when it has to be filled in as a named token, not remembered as an ad hoc style tweak
Disabled states should never use tokens at all, only inline styles
It's purely a performance optimization, unrelated to consistency
items.explanation: Making the disabled state a first-class, named component token (rather than an improvised opacity tweak per screen) is what turns 'remember to handle this' into 'this slot exists and has to be filled in' — closing exactly the gap that let checkout's disabled button drift from every other screen's version.
items.reference:
Component tokens: narrow blast radius, one component, changes often.

Global tokens: wide blast radius, everything downstream, changes rarely and deliberately.

items.prompt: Northwind has a full token catalog (colors, radii, spacing all named and defined) but no shared `Button` component — every squad still assembles their own button markup by hand, referencing the tokens. Is this enough to prevent drift?
choices: Yes — as long as the tokens are correct, drift is impossible

No — a squad can still correctly use `--button-radius` on three screens and forget it on a fourth, or omit the disabled-state token under deadline pressure; tokens fix the *value* problem but not the *assembly* problem
Yes, but only if there are fewer than 10 screens
No, because tokens should never be used without a component library at all
items.explanation: Tokens guarantee that when a value is used, it's the correct shared value — but nothing forces every consumer to use every relevant token, together, correctly, every time. A component library removes that remaining degree of freedom by bundling the whole correct set into one reusable implementation.

Tokens aloneTokens + components
Correct value used?If rememberedAlways (built in)
Full set used together?Not guaranteedGuaranteed

items.prompt: What's the most accurate way to describe the relationship between tokens and components?
choices: Components are a nice-to-have; tokens alone are the real design system

Tokens are the values a design system standardizes; components are what forces every screen to actually consume the full, correct set of those values together, rather than reassembling them by hand each time
Tokens and components solve entirely unrelated problems
Components exist only for accessibility reasons, unrelated to tokens
items.explanation: Tokens and components are two layers of the same fix, not competing approaches: tokens remove ambiguity about *what value* to use, components remove ambiguity about *whether every relevant value got used correctly*. Northwind's checkout bug shows what's left over when only the first layer exists.

items.prompt: Northwind's checkout disabled-state bug happened even though a `color.text.default` alias token already existed. What does that tell you about tokens as a complete fix?
choices: It proves tokens don't work and should be abandoned

It shows tokens can exist correctly while still being skipped or misapplied by a hand-assembled component — the token being right didn't guarantee the checkout button's markup actually used it consistently with every other screen
It proves the token catalog was wrong, not the component
It shows the bug was unrelated to the token/component distinction entirely
items.explanation: The bug wasn't a bad token — it was a component rebuilt from memory that didn't correctly apply the tokens that already existed. That gap between 'correct tokens exist' and 'every component correctly uses them' is precisely what a shared component library closes.

items.prompt: A teammate proposes a stricter code-review checklist ('did you check the disabled state matches other screens?') as the fix for the checkout bug. What does this fix, and what does it leave untouched?
choices: It fixes everything permanently — checklists are a complete substitute for shared components

It can catch this specific failure mode if a reviewer remembers to apply it, but it leaves the root condition — four independent Button implementations — exactly as fragile, requiring the same correct human judgment on every future change, forever
It fixes nothing at all and should never be used
It only works for accessibility bugs, not visual ones
items.explanation: A checklist is a compensating control, not a structural fix — it depends on a person remembering to run it correctly, every time, on every relevant change. A shared component removes the need for that vigilance on this specific axis by making there be only one implementation to get right in the first place.

items.prompt: Why is 'the engineer should have looked harder' the wrong conclusion for the post-mortem to reach?
choices: Because the engineer involved was actually blameless in every respect and no lessons apply to them

Because 'look harder' asks an individual to manually cross-reference three other codebases under deadline pressure, on every future change — a process failure that will recur with the next engineer and the next component, not a one-time lapse
Because engineers should never be asked to review their own work
Because post-mortems should never discuss individual actions
items.explanation: The post-mortem's job is to find the condition that made the mistake likely, not to find someone to blame for one instance of it. 'Look harder' doesn't change that condition — the next engineer building the next component under the next deadline faces the identical setup, absent a structural fix.

items.prompt: Which of these best distinguishes a 'process failure' from a 'diligence failure' in the context of Northwind's checkout bug?
choices: There's no real difference between the two terms

A diligence failure means one person didn't try hard enough; a process failure means the setup made the mistake likely regardless of how hard any one person tried — Northwind's bug was the latter, since there was no shared source of truth to check against
A process failure only applies to backend bugs, never to UI bugs
A diligence failure is always more serious than a process failure
items.explanation: The distinction matters because it changes the fix: a diligence failure suggests 'try harder next time,' while a process failure requires changing the conditions themselves. With four independent Button implementations and no shared source of truth, the setup — not any one engineer's effort — was the actual cause.

items.prompt: Why did Northwind's rollout extract and publish tokens *before* building any shared components, rather than building components first?
choices: It was an arbitrary choice with no real reasoning behind it

Publishing tokens first is low-risk because nothing consumes them yet — nothing can break — while building components first would mean building on top of values that hadn't been agreed on yet, risking rework
Tokens are legally required to ship before components in every company
Components can't technically be built without tokens existing in a database first
items.explanation: Shipping tokens before anything depends on them is a genuinely reversible, low-stakes step — if the chosen blue turns out wrong, only the token needs adjusting. Building components on unstable values first would risk having to rebuild them once the 'real' primary color was settled, wasting the incremental-rollout goal entirely.
items.reference:
1. Extract tokens from values already in use — low risk, nothing consumes them yet
2. Build highest-collision components first (Button, Input, Card)
3. Migrate opportunistically, not all at once
4. Track adoption and incidents together

items.prompt: Northwind built `Button`, `Input`, and `Card` first, ahead of less-used components. What criterion drove that choice?
choices: Alphabetical order
Highest collision — these were the components most duplicated and drifted across screens, so fixing them first addressed the most existing inconsistency per unit of effort
Whichever component the CEO personally used most
Random selection to keep the rollout unbiased
items.explanation: Prioritizing by collision rate — how many independent, drifted implementations of the same idea already existed — targets the rollout at where the existing pain is concentrated, rather than spending early effort on a rarely-duplicated component that wasn't causing real problems.
items.reference:
1. Extract tokens from values already in use — low risk, nothing consumes them yet
2. Build highest-collision components first (Button, Input, Card)
3. Migrate opportunistically, not all at once
4. Track adoption and incidents together

items.prompt: Instead of a dedicated migration sprint, Northwind required new screens to use the new components immediately and let old screens migrate 'opportunistically' — whenever a squad was already touching that screen for other work. What's the benefit of that choice over a big-bang migration?
choices: There's no benefit — a dedicated migration sprint is always strictly better

It avoids freezing the product roadmap for a rewrite, spreads the migration cost across work that was happening anyway, and still guarantees the new-screen surface never grows the old drift problem further
Opportunistic migration means the old bug patterns keep spreading indefinitely with no plan to stop them
It's cheaper only because it skips testing the new components entirely
items.explanation: A big-bang rewrite competes directly with feature work and delays the payoff. Requiring new screens to use the new system stops the problem from growing, while opportunistic migration of old screens converts otherwise-unrelated maintenance work into steady, low-friction progress on the backlog — without a dedicated sprint that has to be separately justified.
items.reference:
1. Extract tokens from values already in use — low risk, nothing consumes them yet
2. Build highest-collision components first (Button, Input, Card)
3. Migrate opportunistically, not all at once
4. Track adoption and incidents together

items.prompt: Northwind's governance model lets any squad *propose* a new component token, but only the design system team can *merge* it. Why not let squads merge their own proposals directly, since they're closest to the problem?
choices: Because squads are never trusted to have good ideas

Because merging without a central review gate recreates the original drift problem one level up — five squads independently editing shared tokens/components reproduces exactly the lack of a single source of truth that caused the checkout bug
Because only the design system team is legally allowed to write CSS
There's no real reason — it's just an arbitrary process rule
items.explanation: The proposal/merge split keeps the system responsive (squads who see the problem first can suggest the fix) while preserving the one property that was missing before the design system existed: a single point that sees every change in context. Removing the merge gate would just relocate the original problem into the shared library itself.

Propose

Any squad — closest to the real need

Merge

Design system team — sees every change in context

items.prompt: Global and alias token changes go through a written RFC before shipping, while component tokens have a lighter review. What justifies treating these differently?
choices: Nothing — all token changes should go through the exact same process regardless of scope

A global/alias change fans out to everything downstream (the whole point of the layering from L2), so it deserves proportionally more scrutiny before shipping than a change scoped to one component's slot
Global tokens are simply harder to write in JSON, requiring more process
RFCs are only used for marketing decisions, not technical ones
items.explanation: Review rigor should scale with blast radius. items.prompt: When `Button`'s API changed to require a new `loadingState` prop, Northwind kept the old prop shape working (with a warning) for one release cycle instead of removing it immediately. Why?
choices: To make the codebase permanently messier by keeping old code paths forever

Because from each squad's point of view, the shared component library is a dependency they didn't choose to have break under them — an immediate silent removal would fail their builds with no warning or migration window
Because removing old props is technically impossible in any framework
It was purely a marketing decision, unrelated to engineering
items.explanation: Treating the internal component library like any other dependency means breaking changes get the same courtesy a public library would offer: a deprecation warning and a migration window, not a silent swap that breaks consuming code without notice — exactly what a well-governed shared system owes the teams that rely on it.

items.prompt: What's the key difference between a 'silently swapped' breaking change and a 'deprecated' one?
choices: There's no meaningful difference — both eventually remove the old behavior

A silent swap replaces the old behavior immediately with no warning, breaking any code still depending on it; a deprecation keeps the old behavior working (with a warning) for a defined window, giving consumers time to migrate before removal
Deprecation means the change never actually happens
Silent swaps are always faster to implement and therefore always preferable
items.explanation: The distinction is entirely about whether consumers get warning and time. A silent swap optimizes for the component owner's convenience at the expense of every consumer's stability; deprecation trades a little extra maintenance overhead for consumers being able to migrate on their own schedule instead of being broken without notice.

items.prompt: In Northwind's Q1-to-Q5 chart, adoption climbs from 10% to 95% while incidents per month fall from 14 to 2. What does showing both series together accomplish that showing only the adoption bars would not?
choices: Nothing extra — the adoption numbers alone are just as convincing

It ties the investment to a measurable outcome (fewer real incidents like the checkout bug), turning 'we rolled out a design system' into a demonstrated result rather than an activity metric leadership has to take on faith
It proves adoption caused the incident drop with certainty, the same way a controlled experiment would
It only matters for the design team's own morale, not for funding decisions
items.explanation: Adoption alone is an activity metric — it shows effort, not payoff. Pairing it with incidents (the same kind of costly, measurable failure the checkout bug represents) is what let Northwind argue the rollout was worth funding further, since it shows the metric that actually matters improving alongside the rollout.
items.reference:
Bars = adoption % across screens (rising). Line = inconsistency incidents/month (falling).

Why: adoption is effort; incidents falling is the actual payoff that justifies the investment.

items.prompt: If Northwind's adoption chart showed adoption rising to 95% but incidents staying flat at 14/month, what would that most likely suggest?
choices: That the chart itself is broken and should be ignored

That something in the rollout isn't actually fixing the root cause — for example, components being adopted without the tokens they should be built from, or the incident categories being tracked not matching what the rollout targets
That incidents and adoption are always unrelated and shouldn't be compared
That the company should immediately abandon the design system
items.explanation: A rollout that isn't reducing the problem it exists to solve is a signal to investigate, not to ignore — maybe adoption is being counted loosely, maybe the incidents being logged aren't the kind the new components actually prevent. The point of tracking both together is exactly to catch a mismatch like this early.

items.prompt: Adding a `variant="danger"` option to `Button` required a new `color.red.500` global token and a new `color.danger` alias — but no existing token was edited. Why does that matter?
choices: It doesn't matter — editing existing tokens would have been just as safe

Because it's an addition, not a modification — every other screen using `Button`'s default variant is completely unaffected, and `color.primary` was never touched, so this change can't reintroduce drift into anything that already worked
Because new tokens are always free of any review process
Because red buttons are technically not covered by design systems
items.explanation: Extending the system by adding new, appropriately-scoped tokens (rather than repurposing or editing an existing one) keeps changes additive: nothing that currently depends on `color.primary` or the default `Button` variant is put at risk by a new, unrelated use case being added alongside it.
items.reference:
New: color.red.500, color.danger — added, not edited.

Untouched: color.primary and every screen using it.

Why: extension, not modification, is what keeps growth safe.
